title: Atomic commit across machines: two-phase commit and XA
goal: By the end, you can explain why one change saved on two machines can lose money, run two-phase commit by hand in PostgreSQL, build the program in charge of it so that it recovers from its own crash, say what waiting for a dead one costs, and tell when XA, a Percolator-style commit or a saga fits.

warmup.q: Here's a careful plan for the 30.00. A program asks both databases: "Can you save your half? If you say yes, you must save it whenever I say so, even after a crash." Both say yes. The program writes "go" in its own notebook on disk, tells the wallets database to save, and crashes before it tells the second one. What does the second database do with its half, and with the row it was changing?
options: After a while it throws its half away, so other payments can change that row again
After a while it saves its half on its own, since it said yes
It keeps its half unsaved and keeps that row blocked until someone tells it the answer, even if it restarts
It asks the wallets database what happened and saves its half, because the two databases sort this out between them
warmup.why: When it said yes, the second database gave up its right to say no later, so it can't throw its half away. It can't save it on its own either, because it doesn't know what the program decided: for all it knows, the other database said no and the answer was "stop". So it waits, and it keeps the row blocked while it waits, through a restart too. Throwing the half away after a timeout is the tempting answer, and here it would leave your wallet debited with no credit anywhere. The two databases don't talk to each other about this; only the program in charge, or a person, can finish it. The plan is called two-phase commit, and the third section measures what that waiting costs.

sections.h: One payment, two databases, and 30.00 that disappears
sections.body:
Let's set up the app behind the café. Each customer keeps money in a wallet inside the app, and each shop has a balance: the money the app's company owes it. When you pay for a coffee, 30.00 moves from your wallet to the shop's balance.

The company keeps both in PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run. A database keeps records in tables, much like the sheets of a spreadsheet, and each record is a row. The wallets sit on one PostgreSQL server, a computer running the database, called `wallets`. The shops' balances sit on another, `payouts`. Your wallet is the row `w-17`, with 100.00 in it. The café is `m-cafe`, with 0.00 so far. (The labs call shops merchants, so shop ids start with `m-`.)

On one server, this would be easy. A transaction is a group of changes that the database treats as one: all of them happen, or none do. You start one with `BEGIN` and end it with `COMMIT`, the moment its changes become permanent. What a transaction promises: ACID and isolation levels, lesson 1 of this track, put that moment in one place. The database first writes every change to its write-ahead log, a file on disk that it only ever adds to, like a notebook. The commit happens when one line, the commit record, reaches that file. A crash before it undoes everything; a crash after it undoes nothing.

Our payment has two halves on two servers: a debit on `wallets` and a credit on `payouts`. Both must happen, or neither. But no single disk holds both rows, so no single line can commit both.

The first version commits one side, then the other: debit `w-17` and COMMIT, then credit `m-cafe` and COMMIT. Now list what can happen in between. The credit can break a constraint, a rule `payouts` checks on every change. The network to `payouts` can drop. `payouts` can crash before its commit record reaches disk. The program running the payment can be stopped halfway. Each time, you've paid 30.00 and the café got nothing.

You may be thinking, "Then undo the debit." But once `wallets` has committed, other programs may have acted on the new balance, say by approving your next purchase against 70.00. Putting the money back is a new transaction, a refund, and it can fail too. Sending both commits at the same moment doesn't help either: one server can still say no, or die, while the other says yes.

The fix needs two ideas. First, nobody commits until everybody has promised that they can. Each server does all its work, checks every rule, saves the changes to disk, and only then gives up its right to say no. Second, one place writes the decision to disk before anyone is told. A change saved so that it survives a crash is called durable. In the figure, the program in charge is the coordinator, and each server holding part of the data is a participant.

**Every participant promises, one durable record decides, then everyone commits.** That's the picture for this lesson, and it has a name: two-phase commit. Next, we'll build it one message at a time.

try.title: Lose 30.00 between two commits
steps: From the `labs` folder, start PostgreSQL with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`. Docker is a program that runs small, separate machines, called containers, on your laptop; this starts one with PostgreSQL 18 inside. Then open psql, PostgreSQL's own prompt for typing SQL, the language you ask a database things in: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`. One server stands in for two machines here. PostgreSQL can't run one transaction across two databases, even on one server, so `wallets` and `payouts` are as separate as two servers would be.

Run the setup, then the payment. `\c` closes the current connection and opens one to the named database. When it closes `payouts` before the COMMIT, that's the program running the payment dying halfway.
Predict both balances before you read them. Amounts are kept in cents (`balance_minor`), so 10000 is 100.00.

code.title: one psql session

try.expect:
```text
 balance_minor
---------------
          7000
(1 row)

You are now connected to database "payouts" as user "sfz".
 balance_minor
---------------
             0
(1 row)
```

(Setup output trimmed.) The debit committed on `wallets`. The credit was still inside an open transaction when its connection closed, so PostgreSQL rolled it back, which means it undid it, exactly as it would after a crash. You paid 30.00 and the café got nothing, and neither server did anything wrong: each kept its own promise about its own data.

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: Reliability and the write-ahead log

sections.h: Two-phase commit: everyone promises first, then one line in a log decides
sections.body:
Picture organising a dinner for three friends by text. You ask each one: "Friday at eight? If you say yes, keep the evening free." Only when all three have said yes do you write "dinner is on" in your diary and text everyone. If anyone says no, you text "off".

Two-phase commit (2PC) works the same way. The **coordinator** is you: the program that runs the transaction and decides how it ends. It's often a library inside the program that makes the payment, called a transaction manager. The **participants** are the friends: the servers that hold the data, here `wallets` and `payouts`. The transaction gets one id that everyone shares, here `txf-1`.

Phase one is prepare. The coordinator sends each participant its changes, then asks it to prepare. A participant that can commit writes all its changes, plus a line that says "prepared", to its write-ahead log, and makes sure they're on disk. Then it answers yes. That yes is a promise: whatever happens next, even a crash and a restart, it will commit if told to. So it may no longer give up on its own, and it keeps every lock the transaction took. A lock is a mark on a row that stops other transactions from changing it until this one ends; Concurrency control: locks, deadlocks and SSI (lesson 5) met them. That's the friend keeping Friday free. A participant that can't commit, because a rule failed or its disk is full, rolls back, undoing its changes, and answers no.

Then the coordinator decides. If every answer is yes, it adds `txf-1 COMMIT` to its own log and waits until the disk has it. **That one line is the commit point** of the whole transaction, the moment it counts as committed. It's the note in your diary. If any answer is no, or doesn't arrive in time, it decides abort: it calls the whole thing off.

Phase two is commit. The coordinator tells every participant the outcome. After a commit decision it keeps trying each participant until each one confirms, for minutes or days if it must, because it can't take the decision back.

Notice the two points of no return. A participant's yes takes away its right to abort. The coordinator's line takes away everyone's. An abort needs no line at all: a transaction the log doesn't mention is treated as aborted, which is called **presumed abort**. That's safe because nobody can have committed without the line.

PostgreSQL can be a participant. `PREPARE TRANSACTION 'txf-1@wallets'` ends your session's transaction (a session is one connection to the database) without finishing it. It lives on as a prepared transaction, holding its locks, listed in `pg_prepared_xacts`. Later, any session connected to the same database finishes it with `COMMIT PREPARED` or `ROLLBACK PREPARED`. The feature is off by default: the setting `max_prepared_transactions` is 0, and changing it needs a restart. The docs say it's meant for transaction managers, not ordinary programs.

Count the cost. A round trip is the time for a message to go and its answer to come back. A normal commit is one round trip and one wait for the disk. Two-phase commit needs two round trips to every participant, and three disk waits in a row: the prepare lines, the decision, then the commits. Between data centres at two ends of a continent, a round trip takes about 70 ms (thousandths of a second). So each payment would spend about 140 ms on the network instead of 70.

Next, we'll stop the coordinator at the worst moment.

stepper.intro: The coordinator moves 30.00 from `w-17` on `wallets` to `m-cafe` on `payouts`. The bottom line shows what someone reading both servers would see. Use Next and Back, or the arrow keys.

frames.say: Phase two. The coordinator sends `COMMIT PREPARED` to `wallets`, which commits and releases its lock. For a moment, someone reading both servers sees the debit without the credit. Two-phase commit makes the outcome all or nothing. It doesn't make both servers show it at the same instant.

The coordinator writes nothing and sends `ROLLBACK PREPARED` to `wallets`. A payment with no line in the log is treated as aborted: that's **presumed abort**. A participant that doesn't answer in time counts as a no, as long as the decision hasn't been written yet.

try.title: Run two-phase commit by hand
steps: In the psql prompt (connected to `wallets`), try to prepare a transaction. It fails, and the failed PREPARE rolls the transaction back. The `ALTER SYSTEM` line switches the feature on for the next start. Restart the server from the `labs` folder: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml restart db`.

Open two terminals, windows where you type commands. Connect terminal 1 to `wallets` with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d wallets`, and terminal 2 to `payouts` with `-d payouts` at the end instead. You're the coordinator now. Run phase one in both, then look at `pg_prepared_xacts`. Each participant gets its own id, such as `txf-1@wallets`, because both databases sit on one server and an id must be unique on the whole server. Predict what terminal 1's SELECT shows right after its PREPARE.
Run phase two: commit each prepared transaction. Terminal 1 commits from a new statement, after its own transaction has ended: any session in the right database can finish a prepared transaction.

code.title: two psql sessions

try.expect:
The first PREPARE fails:

```text
ERROR:  prepared transactions are disabled
HINT:  Set "max_prepared_transactions" to a nonzero value.
```

After the restart, `SHOW` prints 10. Terminal 1's PREPARE prints `PREPARE TRANSACTION`, and its SELECT then shows `10000`. The session is no longer in a transaction, and the prepared change is invisible to everyone, itself included, until it commits. Terminal 2 lists both:

```text
      gid      | database |           prepared
---------------+----------+-------------------------------
 txf-1@payouts | payouts  | 2026-11-08 05:39:20.755114+00
 txf-1@wallets | wallets  | 2026-11-08 05:39:20.604174+00
(2 rows)
```

`pg_prepared_xacts` shows the whole server, every database on it. Each `COMMIT PREPARED` prints `COMMIT PREPARED`, terminal 1 then reads `7000`, and the count is 0. Your timestamps will differ.

sections.h: When the coordinator dies: participants wait in doubt and keep their locks
sections.body:
Now the failure the protocol was built around. Both servers voted yes, and then the coordinator's program dies before it tells anyone the outcome. `payouts` promised to commit if told to, and nobody is telling it anything. A participant in that state is **in doubt**. It's the friend who said yes to Friday, a moment before the organiser's phone died. Here the dinner picture breaks: a friend would ring around within a day, while a participant waits, blocking its rows, for as long as it takes.

Can it decide on its own? Committing is unsafe: for all it knows, `wallets` voted no, and the coordinator decided abort. Aborting is unsafe too: maybe the coordinator wrote its COMMIT line and `wallets` has already committed. Asking `wallets` helps only if `wallets` has committed. If it's also only prepared, neither knows whether the line exists. So an in-doubt participant waits for the coordinator. That makes two-phase commit a **blocking** protocol: one dead coordinator can stop the participants for as long as it stays dead.

While it waits, it holds its locks. Plain reads still work. PostgreSQL keeps old versions of each row, as MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM (lesson 4) showed, so a reader sees the last committed version without waiting. But every writer that touches an in-doubt row, `w-17` or `m-cafe`, waits behind the prepared transaction until its own `lock_timeout`, the longest it may wait for a lock, runs out. Every purchase at the café would wait.

Three more things make it worse. `pg_blocking_pids`, which names the process a waiting session is stuck behind, reports process 0: a prepared transaction belongs to no session, so there's no session to stop. VACUUM, PostgreSQL's cleaner for old row versions, can't remove any version replaced after the prepared transaction started, because that transaction counts as still running. And restarting doesn't help. The prepared transaction is on disk and comes back at startup with its locks (`recovering prepared transaction 767`, says the server's log).

How long does this last? As long as the coordinator is gone. If it restarts in 20 seconds, that's 20 seconds of blocked rows. If its disk is lost, it lasts until a person picks an outcome by hand, what the next section's XA standard calls a heuristic decision.

The wrong guess is tempting. Picture someone who finds a prepared transaction that has blocked the café's row for an hour, and rolls it back to free the row. If the coordinator had decided commit and `wallets` had committed, the payment is now half done, and nothing will ever report it. Before finishing anything by hand, read the coordinator's log, or check what the other participant did with the same id.

So recovery is the coordinator's first job when it starts again. It reads its log, asks every participant for its in-doubt ids (`pg_prepared_xacts` in PostgreSQL), commits the ones its log says COMMIT, and rolls back the rest. That's the lab. It works only if the log never forgets a decision it acted on. Had the COMMIT line not reached disk before the first `COMMIT PREPARED` went out, a crash could lose it after one side committed. Recovery would then roll back the other side. That's why the lab's `recordCommit` calls `force(true)`, which makes the operating system put the line on disk before it returns.

Every participant so far has been PostgreSQL. Next, we'll mix products, and see why most teams stay away.

try.title: Leave a payment in doubt
steps: Terminals 1 and 2 play the coordinator again, and this time it dies after phase one: prepare `txf-2` on both, and don't commit. Open terminal 3 on `wallets` and change `w-17`, as another payment from the same wallet would. It waits.

In terminal 1, find out who terminal 3 waits for. Then make some old row versions on `w-18` (each UPDATE leaves one behind) and run VACUUM. Predict whether VACUUM can remove them. Watch terminal 3 give up after 10 seconds.

Restart the server from the `labs` folder (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml restart db`), reconnect terminal 1 and check `pg_prepared_xacts` again. Then finish both the way the coordinator's log would: commit.

code.title: three psql sessions

try.expect:
Terminal 1 sees terminal 3 waiting, blocked by process 0, and the prepared transactions' locks with no process id (pid):

```text
 pid | blocked_by |  wait_event
-----+------------+---------------
  85 | {0}        | transactionid

 pid |   locktype    | xid |     mode      | granted
-----+---------------+-----+---------------+---------
     | transactionid | 767 | ExclusiveLock | t
     | transactionid | 768 | ExclusiveLock | t
  85 | transactionid | 769 | ExclusiveLock | t
  85 | transactionid | 767 | ShareLock     | f

      gid      | transaction
---------------+-------------
 txf-2@payouts |         768
 txf-2@wallets |         767
```

Terminal 3 waits on transaction 767, which is `txf-2@wallets`. VACUUM can't clean up behind it (output trimmed to two lines):

```text
tuples: 4 removed, 5 remain, 3 are dead but not yet removable
removable cutoff: 767, which was 6 XIDs old when operation ended
```

After 10 seconds terminal 3 fails with `ERROR:  canceling statement due to lock timeout`. After the restart both ids are still listed, and the server log says `recovering prepared transaction 767 from shared memory`. The first `COMMIT PREPARED` fails with `ERROR:  prepared transaction belongs to another database`: you finish a prepared transaction from its own database. Then both commit, and `w-17` reads `4000`. Your pids and ids will differ.

sections.h: XA: two-phase commit between different products, and why most teams avoid it
sections.body:
In many companies the second participant is another product. It might be Oracle, a database program many banks run, or a message queue, a program that holds messages until another program collects them, such as IBM MQ or ActiveMQ. Two-phase commit across different products needs one shared way to say prepare, commit and roll back. The standard one is **X/Open XA**, written in 1991 by a group of computer makers. XA isn't a network protocol. It's an API, a set of functions, between a transaction manager and each resource, which is any program that holds data and can take part.

In Java, XA appears as JTA, the Java Transaction API. Each resource hands the transaction manager an `XAResource` with `start`, `end`, `prepare`, `commit`, `rollback` and `recover`. Every branch, one participant's share of the transaction, is named by an `Xid`. It holds a format id, a global transaction id and a branch qualifier, the same "one id per participant" idea as `txf-1@wallets`. Narayana, a free transaction manager for Java, runs inside the program itself and writes its decisions to a folder on that machine's disk. pgJDBC, the library Java programs use to talk to PostgreSQL, turns `prepare` into `PREPARE TRANSACTION`. The Try it plays Narayana by hand.

Most teams that try XA for real end up avoiding it, for four reasons.

1. The coordinator is the program itself, and its log sits on that machine's disk. Many companies run programs on machines that get replaced at any time, each with an empty disk; Kubernetes, a popular system for running programs on many machines, works that way. Replace the machine, and the log is gone. The in-doubt branches in Oracle then wait for a database administrator, the person who looks after the database, to decide by hand.
2. Each resource sees only its own locks. Say transaction A holds a row in Oracle and waits for a row in PostgreSQL that transaction B holds, while B waits for A's Oracle row. That's a deadlock: each waits for the other, forever. Neither database sees the whole circle, so lesson 5's deadlock detector never fires, and only a timeout ends it.
3. Every transaction pays the extra round trips and disk waits, and every lock is held until the slowest participant has prepared.
4. Much of what a payment touches doesn't speak XA at all. Redis (the Caching track's in-memory store) doesn't, nor does DynamoDB (Amazon's database service, next lesson), a card company's web service or an email. Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages, has an accepted proposal to join in (KIP-939), still not in a release in November 2026.

XA keeps a coordinator that one crash can stop. Next, we'll look at two designs that get rid of it.

try.title: Run XA by hand, then recover
steps: This uses the `wallets` and `payouts` databases from the earlier Try its, with prepared transactions switched on. Read `XaDemo.kt`. For each database it calls `start`, runs the UPDATE, then calls `end` and `prepare`. Then it closes its connections without committing: the coordinator dies. Last, it plays the restarted transaction manager: `recover` on each resource, then `commit`.
Before you run it, predict what the ids in `pg_prepared_xacts` look like. The demo's Xid has format id 1001, global id `txf-7`, and the database name as the branch.
Run it from the `labs` folder. Then run it a second time: is anything left from the first run to recover?

code.title: XaDemo.kt (the two phases)

try.expect:
```text
== phase 1: start, work, end and prepare each branch of txf-7
wallets  prepare -> XA_OK, a yes vote
payouts  prepare -> XA_OK, a yes vote
== what PostgreSQL holds now
payouts  1001_dHhmLTc=_cGF5b3V0cw==
wallets  1001_dHhmLTc=_d2FsbGV0cw==
== recovery: a restarted transaction manager asks each resource what is in doubt
wallets  in doubt: formatId 1001, global id txf-7, branch wallets
wallets  commit -> done
payouts  in doubt: formatId 1001, global id txf-7, branch payouts
payouts  commit -> done
w-17 is now 2500
```

pgJDBC writes the Xid into the id: the format id, then the global id and the branch in Base64, a way of writing any bytes as plain letters and digits (`dHhmLTc=` is `txf-7`). `recover` reads them back from `pg_prepared_xacts` and decodes them. That list is all a restarted transaction manager learns from the database. Whether to commit has to come from its own log; this demo commits without checking. The second run recovers only its own branches, since the first run left nothing behind, and `w-17` reads `1000`. Each run moves 15.00.

refs.title: Quarkus: using transactions (Narayana, XA and recovery)

aside.title: Couldn't a third round of messages remove the waiting?
aside.body: That's three-phase commit (3PC). It adds a round so that a participant that hears nothing can decide on its own after a timeout. That's safe only if every message and every pause has a known upper limit, so that silence really means the coordinator is dead. Real networks have no such limit, as the Faults, time and truth track shows: a slow coordinator looks exactly like a dead one, and two participants that time out at different moments can decide differently. So systems that need all or nothing across machines keep two-phase commit and make the coordinator survive crashes instead. They keep its log on several machines that agree on every line, which is called consensus; Google's Spanner and CockroachDB work this way, as the Consistency and consensus track shows.

sections.h: Two ways around the coordinator: keep the decision with the data, or give up on one commit
sections.body:
The weak spot of two-phase commit is the coordinator: a separate program holding the one record that decides, which every participant must wait for. There are two ways around it.

The first moves the decision into the data. Google's Percolator, from 2010, kept the index behind Google's web search up to date. It ran on Bigtable, Google's huge table store, which can change only one row at a time all or nothing. A Percolator transaction locks every cell it writes (a cell is one value in a row) and picks one of those locks as the **primary**. Every other lock points to it. To commit, the client, the program running the transaction, replaces the primary lock with a commit record, in one single-row write. That write is the commit point. It does the job of our log line, but it sits next to the data, where any reader can find it.

If the client dies before cleaning up its other locks, the next reader that meets one follows the pointer to the primary. A commit record there means finish the write, which is called rolling it forward. No commit record, and nobody still working on it, means roll it back. Nobody waits for a coordinator to return, because there is no separate coordinator.

The price is paid elsewhere. A transaction that runs into a dead client's lock must clean it up first, and the paper says this can delay a commit by tens of seconds. That was fine for a search index, and far too slow for buying a coffee. Percolator also allows the write skew of Write skew and phantoms (lesson 3): two transactions each check a rule, then each change a different row.

The second way gives up atomic commit and keeps the business rule. Durable execution: workflows that survive crashes, in the Encoding, APIs and workflows track, met workflow engines, programs that run a job of several steps to the end through crashes. A **saga**, an idea from Garcia-Molina and Salem in 1987, is such a job made of local transactions, each with a compensating step that undoes its effect. Our payment becomes three steps. Debit `w-17` and record the payment as pending, in one local transaction on `wallets`. Credit `m-cafe` with a payout entry keyed by the payment's id, in one local transaction on `payouts`. Mark the payment done. If the credit can never succeed, the compensation refunds `w-17`. Each step commits alone, so nothing is ever in doubt and no lock outlives its step. Each step is also idempotent: running it twice has the same effect as running it once, so the engine can retry it safely.

What you give up is isolation, the promise that transactions don't see each other's half-done work. Between the steps, anyone can see the debit without the credit: lesson 1's dirty read, seeing work nobody has committed, at the size of a business. And a compensation is a new action, not a rollback. The refund shows on your statement, and an email already sent stays sent. So make "pending" a real state that reports and support staff understand.

**Choose by where the participants live.** Inside one database that spreads over many machines, let its own commit protocol do the work. Across separate programs and products, use a saga with idempotency keys, a unique id per payment that makes a repeated step do nothing. Keep XA for when every participant supports it, the coordinator's log is durable and backed up, and few transactions want the same rows.

refs.title: Peng and Dabek: Large-scale incremental processing using distributed transactions and notifications (Percolator, OSDI 2010)

compare.title: One payment two ways: two-phase commit and a saga

a.label: Two-phase commit
a.title: one distributed transaction
a.src:
wallets: BEGIN, debit w-17           lock w-17
payouts: BEGIN, credit m-cafe        lock m-cafe
wallets: PREPARE  -> yes             w-17 still locked
payouts: PREPARE  -> yes             m-cafe still locked
coordinator log: txf-1 COMMIT        <- commit point
wallets: COMMIT PREPARED             w-17 released
payouts: COMMIT PREPARED             m-cafe released

coordinator dies after prepare:  both rows stay locked
isolation:  nobody sees a debit without its credit*
needs:      XA or PREPARE on every participant

b.label: Saga
b.title: three local transactions in a workflow
b.src:
wallets: debit w-17, transfer txf-1 = pending   commit
payouts: credit m-cafe, entry txf-1             commit
wallets: transfer txf-1 = done                  commit
if the credit can never succeed:
wallets: refund w-17, txf-1 = refunded          commit

workflow dies between steps:  it resumes; nothing locked
isolation:  anyone can see txf-1 pending
needs:      idempotent steps and a durable workflow

compare.note: Two-phase commit keeps the payment all or nothing and holds locks on both servers until the end, so a dead coordinator freezes rows. A saga commits each step at once, so nothing is ever in doubt and nothing stays locked. But the in-between state is visible, and undoing means a new step, a refund, instead of a rollback. *Even two-phase commit shows half the payment for a moment to someone reading both servers, between the two COMMIT PREPAREDs, as the stepper showed.

worked.title: Recover after a crash: decide every in-doubt branch

steps.say: Gather what the restarted coordinator can see: its own log, and the list of prepared transactions on each participant.
steps.code:
coordinator.log           wallets: pg_prepared_xacts      payouts: pg_prepared_xacts
txf-4 COMMIT              txf-5@wallets                   txf-5@payouts
txf-5 COMMIT              txf-6@wallets                   txf-6@payouts
                          batch-9@ledger

steps.say: Apply one rule to each id. Our ids end with `@<participant>`. A COMMIT line for the payment's id means commit. No line means the coordinator never decided commit, so no participant can have committed, and rolling back is safe. An id from another coordinator isn't ours to touch.
steps.code:
txf-5@wallets    log says COMMIT     -> COMMIT PREPARED
txf-6@wallets    no line             -> ROLLBACK PREPARED   (presumed abort)
batch-9@ledger   not ours            -> leave it alone
txf-5@payouts    log says COMMIT     -> COMMIT PREPARED
txf-6@payouts    no line             -> ROLLBACK PREPARED
txf-4            nothing prepared    -> already finished before the crash

steps.say: Write it as code. The loop is short because the hard part, deciding, was done before the crash and written down.

Check why the order of steps in `run` makes this safe. The COMMIT line reaches disk after every yes and before the first COMMIT PREPARED. If the coordinator wrote it after sending the commits, a crash could lose the line while one side had committed, and this loop would roll the other side back.
steps.code:
safe:    prepare all -> fsync "txf-5 COMMIT" -> COMMIT PREPARED wallets -> COMMIT PREPARED payouts
unsafe:  prepare all -> COMMIT PREPARED wallets -> crash (line never written)
         recovery: no line for txf-5 -> ROLLBACK PREPARED txf-5@payouts -> half a transfer

lab.title: Build a two-phase commit coordinator that survives its own crash
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. They start a PostgreSQL 18 container of their own through Testcontainers, a library that starts Docker containers for tests, with `max_prepared_transactions = 10` and two databases, `wallets` and `payouts`. That takes a few seconds, more the first time, while Docker downloads PostgreSQL. All 10 tests fail.

Read `TwoPhaseCommit.kt`. `Participant`, `DecisionLog`, `CrashPoint` and `maybeCrash` are written for you. `CoordinatorCrashed` extends `Error`, so a `catch (e: Exception)` in your code can't hide a crash, in the same way that no catch block runs when a program is killed.

Write `Coordinator.run` from its KDoc, the comment above it. Phase one sends `BEGIN`, the statements and `PREPARE TRANSACTION` to each participant. On a no vote, send `ROLLBACK` to that one and `ROLLBACK PREPARED` to those already prepared. Then write the log line, then send `COMMIT PREPARED`, with the three `maybeCrash` calls in between. Four tests pass. One checks that a writer gets SQLSTATE 55P03 on a row an in-doubt transaction holds: SQLSTATE is PostgreSQL's five-character error code, and 55P03 means a lock wasn't available.
Write `Coordinator.recover`. Four more pass: after a crash before the decision, after it, between the two commits, and with another coordinator's id on the same server.
Fix `in_doubt.sql`, the query you'd run first to see who is stuck behind each in-doubt transaction. It runs, and its numbers are wrong in three ways. The last two tests pass.
hints: Catch only `SQLException` in phase one. `e.sqlState` gives `23505` for the duplicate payout entry and `23514` for the CHECK rule that a wallet balance can't go below zero.

After a failed statement inside BEGIN, `ROLLBACK` ends the failed transaction. After a failed PREPARE, PostgreSQL has already rolled back, and a ROLLBACK only prints a warning, so you can send it either way.
In `recover`, `p.preparedGids()` already keeps only the participant's own database. You still have to keep only the ids that end with `@${p.name}`.

`in_doubt.sql`: make the join a LEFT JOIN, so a transaction nobody waits for keeps its row; count `w.pid`, not `*`; skip granted locks (`NOT w.granted`), because each prepared transaction holds a lock on its own transaction id; and keep only `p.database = current_database()`, because both views cover the whole server.

drill.title: The coordinator's commit path from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write `run(txId, work)` for a coordinator over PostgreSQL participants: phase one, the abort path, the decision and phase two. Then answer: what is the commit point, and why must it come before the first `COMMIT PREPARED`?

recap: On one machine, a commit is one line reaching one log on disk. Across two machines no single write covers both, so committing one side, then the other, loses money whenever the second side fails.

Two-phase commit: every participant prepares (changes on disk, locks kept, a yes or no vote), the coordinator writes one COMMIT line to its log (the commit point), then tells everyone. No line means abort.
PostgreSQL can be a participant: `PREPARE TRANSACTION 'gid'`, `pg_prepared_xacts`, then `COMMIT PREPARED` or `ROLLBACK PREPARED` from the same database. `max_prepared_transactions` is 0 by default.

The limit: if the coordinator dies after the votes, participants are in doubt. They can't decide alone, keep their row locks through restarts, block writers and hold back VACUUM until recovery reads the log, or a person guesses.

XA is two-phase commit across products (JTA in Java). Its log on one machine's disk, deadlocks nobody sees and the many systems without XA make teams avoid it. A third phase doesn't help, because real delays have no upper limit.

Percolator moves the commit point into the data (a primary lock), so any reader can finish a dead client's work. A saga gives up atomic commit for local steps with compensations, and pays with visible in-between states.

quiz.q: A coordinator crashes after both participants voted yes, but before it wrote anything to its log. It restarts with its log intact. What does recovery do with the two prepared branches?
options: Commits both: every participant voted yes, so the payment can go through
Rolls back both: with no COMMIT line, the coordinator never decided commit, so nobody can have committed
Leaves both prepared and waits for a person to decide
Commits the one that prepared first and rolls back the other
quiz.why: This is presumed abort. The COMMIT line is written only after every yes and before any COMMIT PREPARED, so its absence proves that no participant committed. Rolling back both agrees with every participant. Committing both would also be all or nothing here, which makes it tempting. But recovery can't tell this case from one where a third vote never arrived, so the rule has to be abort. Waiting for a person throws away what the log already says.

quiz.q: The café's row in the `payouts` database has been blocked for an hour by a prepared transaction, `txf-5@payouts`. A database administrator runs `ROLLBACK PREPARED 'txf-5@payouts'` so the café can take payments again. The coordinator's log says `txf-5 COMMIT`, and `txf-5@wallets` committed an hour ago. What is the result?
options: Nothing bad: the coordinator will notice and commit it again
The whole payment is rolled back on both servers
Half a payment: the wallet stays debited, the café is never credited, and nothing reports it
The ROLLBACK fails, because only the coordinator may finish its prepared transactions
quiz.why: Once rolled back, the branch is gone. The coordinator's recovery finds no prepared `txf-5@payouts` and has nothing to commit, while `wallets` committed long ago. This is the heuristic decision that breaks all or nothing. PostgreSQL lets a superuser (an account allowed to do anything) or the original user run ROLLBACK PREPARED, so it doesn't fail. The right move was to read the log, or check `wallets`, and run COMMIT PREPARED.

quiz.q: Someone proposes three-phase commit so that participants never wait: one that hears nothing for 5 seconds will decide on its own. What does that rely on?
options: That no message or pause ever takes longer than the timeout, so silence really means the coordinator is dead
That the coordinator's log is copied to other machines
That every participant runs the same database product
Nothing extra: the third phase removes the waiting in every case
quiz.why: The timeout rule is safe only if delays have an upper limit. On a real network, a coordinator that pauses for 6 seconds (say, while Java clears out unused memory) or sits behind a slow link looks dead. Participants that time out at different moments can then reach different decisions. Copying the coordinator's log to machines that agree on it is the fix that works, and it's a different design. The product doesn't matter.

quiz.q: From MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM (lesson 4): a prepared transaction has been in doubt since the weekend. On Monday, VACUUM on a busy table in the same database reports thousands of row versions that "are dead but not yet removable", and the table keeps growing. Why?
options: Prepared transactions switch off autovacuum, the automatic VACUUM, until they finish
The prepared transaction counts as still running, so VACUUM's cutoff can't move past its id, and no version that died after it can be removed
The dead versions belong to the prepared transaction
VACUUM needs the row locks the prepared transaction holds
quiz.why: VACUUM removes an old version only when the transaction that replaced it committed before every transaction still running. A prepared transaction is still running, so the cutoff stays at its id, as the Try it showed with `removable cutoff: 767`, and every version that died since then stays. The dead versions can belong to anyone. Autovacuum still runs, but it can't remove them. That's why the PostgreSQL docs warn against leaving transactions prepared.

quiz.q: From Concurrency control: locks, deadlocks and SSI (lesson 5): two XA transactions run at once. T1 has changed a row in Oracle and now waits for a row in PostgreSQL that T2 changed. T2 now waits for T1's Oracle row. What ends this?
options: PostgreSQL's deadlock detector, after `deadlock_timeout`
Oracle's deadlock detector, which raises ORA-00060
The transaction manager, which joins both databases' lists of who waits for whom
A lock or transaction timeout, because neither database sees a circle: each sees one transaction waiting for another
quiz.why: A deadlock detector searches its own waits-for graph, its record of which transaction waits for which. PostgreSQL sees T1 waiting for T2 and nothing more; Oracle sees T2 waiting for T1. The circle exists only across the two, and XA gives no part the whole picture. So only a timeout breaks it: a lock timeout on either database, or the transaction manager's own transaction timeout. Expecting a local detector to fire is the tempting mistake.

flashcards.front: What does a participant promise when it votes yes in two-phase commit?
flashcards.back: That it can and will commit if told to, even after a crash: its changes and a prepare line are on disk, it keeps its locks, and it can no longer abort on its own.

flashcards.front: What is the commit point of two-phase commit?
flashcards.back: The coordinator's decision line (`txf-1 COMMIT`) reaching its log on disk, after every yes vote and before any participant is told to commit.

flashcards.front: What does `PREPARE TRANSACTION 'gid'` do in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: It ends the session's transaction without finishing it. The work stays on disk with its locks, listed in `pg_prepared_xacts`, until `COMMIT PREPARED` or `ROLLBACK PREPARED` from the same database.

flashcards.front: Why can't an in-doubt participant roll back after a timeout?
flashcards.back: The coordinator may have decided commit, and another participant may have committed already. Rolling back would leave half the transaction. So it waits, holding its locks.
A transaction with no commit line in the coordinator's log is treated as aborted. It's safe because nobody commits until that line exists.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't three-phase commit fix the waiting on real networks?
flashcards.back: It's safe only if message delays and pauses have an upper limit. Without one, a slow coordinator looks dead, and participants can decide differently.

flashcards.front: What does a saga give up compared with two-phase commit?
flashcards.back: Isolation and atomic commit: each step commits alone, others can see the in-between state, and undoing means running a compensating step, not a rollback.

terms.plain: Making a transaction that spans several machines commit on all of them or on none.
Prepare everywhere, write one decision to disk, then commit everywhere. Not the same as two-phase locking.
The program that runs a transaction across machines, collects the votes and writes the decision.
A server that holds part of the data and votes yes or no in the prepare phase.
A participant that voted yes and hasn't learned the outcome. It can't decide alone, and it keeps its locks.
Treating a transaction with no commit line in the coordinator's log as aborted.
The standard set of calls for two-phase commit across different products, and its Java form (`XAResource`, `Xid`).
A chain of local transactions, each with a compensating step that undoes it, run to the end by a workflow engine instead of one atomic commit.

explain_back.prompt: A friend is building an online shop. She wants to save each order in her Oracle database and put a message for the warehouse on IBM MQ, a message queue, in one XA transaction, "so they commit together". Explain what two-phase commit guarantees, what happens if her program dies at the wrong moment, and what you'd suggest instead.
explain_back.answer: XA runs two-phase commit, with a transaction manager such as Narayana inside her program as the coordinator. Oracle and MQ first prepare: each saves its work to disk, keeps its locks and votes yes. Then the coordinator writes one commit line to its log, and from that moment the order is committed; then it tells both to commit. That does make the outcome all or nothing. The catch is the coordinator. If her program dies after both prepared, Oracle keeps the order rows locked and MQ keeps the message in limbo until the coordinator comes back with the same log, and that log is on the program's own disk. If the machine is replaced with a fresh disk, an administrator has to guess the outcome, and a wrong guess breaks the very promise she wanted. Every order would also pay extra round trips and disk waits, and a deadlock between Oracle and MQ wouldn't be seen by either. Instead I'd save the order and a "message to send" row in one local Oracle transaction. A small separate program reads those rows and puts each message on the queue, and the warehouse ignores a message id it has already seen. Each piece commits locally, nothing is ever in doubt, and a crash only delays the message.

deeper.body:
**Making the coordinator survive.** Gray and Lamport's "Consensus on Transaction Commit" (2006) replaces the single coordinator's log with a group of machines, called acceptors, that agree on the outcome with Paxos, a consensus protocol. The decision then survives as long as more than half of them are up. Spanner and CockroachDB go the same way: every participant is itself a group of copies that agree with each other, so a participant never disappears, and the coordinator's state is copied with it. The Consistency and consensus track builds the consensus part.

**Watching for in-doubt work.** Set an alert for any transaction that stays in `pg_prepared_xacts` for more than a minute. A healthy coordinator finishes its prepared transactions in milliseconds, so an old one means a coordinator is gone.

**Shortcuts real transaction managers take.** If only one resource takes part, there is nothing to coordinate: JTA commits it in one phase, `XAResource.commit(xid, true)`. A branch that changed nothing can vote read-only (`XA_RDONLY`) in prepare and skip phase two. Some managers allow a "last resource": one resource without XA, committed in the middle, after the others have prepared. That works until the answer to that one commit is lost on the network.

**Percolator's descendants.** TiDB, a database that spreads SQL tables over many machines, uses a Percolator-style protocol in its storage layer, TiKV.

**What XA can't offer across products.** Lesson 5's serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) catches dangerous patterns by watching which transactions read what others wrote. Across two products, no database sees the other's reads and writes, so XA can't give you SSI either.

**DynamoDB's version.** Lesson 8 of this track opens DynamoDB's transaction protocol: coordinators that record their decisions in a ledger table, and a recovery manager that hands a stalled transaction to another coordinator. It's two-phase commit with the coordinator's log kept in a database with copies on many machines, instead of on one disk.

**The book's framing.** Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 8, covers atomic commit, XA and exactly-once message processing, and explains why many cloud services choose not to offer distributed transactions at all.

sources.title: Peng and Dabek: Large-scale Incremental Processing Using Distributed Transactions and Notifications (OSDI 2010)

opening:
Picture paying for a coffee from the money you keep in a café chain's app, your wallet. The app says it went through, and your wallet drops from 100.00 to 70.00. That evening, the café's owner checks what she's owed for the day. Your 30.00 isn't there.

The wallets live in one database, and the shops' balances in another, on a different machine. The first saved the debit. The second crashed a moment before it saved the credit.

It's easy to think a careful order fixes this: save one side, then the other, and undo the first if the second fails. Each database keeps its own promises perfectly, so two of them together feel as safe.

In Serial execution: Redis MULTI, WATCH and Lua, a transaction that touched two slices of the data ran far slower, or was refused. In this lesson, we'll lose that 30.00 on purpose, build two-phase commit to stop it, kill the program in charge at the worst moment, and weigh the ways around it. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with 30.00 that left a wallet and never reached the café. Two-phase commit stops that: every server promises first, and one line on disk decides. Its price is the wait when the coordinator dies, which is why many payment systems use sagas instead.

If you can reach a PostgreSQL server, run `SHOW max_prepared_transactions;`. A 0 means nobody there uses two-phase commit. Then open your bank's app and look for a transfer marked pending: that's the kind of in-between state a saga shows on purpose.

Next, we'll look at three databases built to spread data over many machines, DynamoDB, MongoDB and Cassandra, and find out what each does when two transactions want the same account at once.
